records.name: Anguilla
records.current_summary:
Anguilla's prohibitions were removed around 2000-2001 — a recent first-person travel account puts the change at 2000, the contemporaneous wire coverage of the Caribbean-wide reform at January 2001 — again by imposition from London after local reluctance; the earlier profile's 'decriminalised 2019' appeared in no source and has been deleted. Same-sex relationships are simply not an issue in the public sense because there is almost no public LGBT life: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers and same-sex wedding tourism pitched on 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere.'

A queer family travelling openly in 2023 described the experience as uneventful on a 35-square-mile island. The practical visitor picture is quiet neutrality — nothing protects you much, and little opposes you at all.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz country report on Anguilla (2012): profile of a 35-square-mile island about 100 miles east of the British Virgin Islands, framing gay life against dependent-territory law — Britain holds ultimate legal authority and decriminalisation came by British order rather than local repeal, with local religious protest against the change; Anguilla never had the exact prohibition law itself in the same form.

Commercial destination-wedding page for Anguilla: states plainly that 'Same-sex marriage is not currently recognized under the law in Anguilla', while marketing the island's venues for ceremonies — useful as a practical marker that only symbolic ceremonies are possible for same-sex couples there.

Associated Press via SodomyLaws (Jan 5, 2001): Britain's Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and Turks and Caicos — acting unilaterally after local legislatures refused to repeal, drawing protests from religious leaders.

AFAR first-person travel piece (Jun 2023): a queer family's visit finds gay sex legal in Anguilla through the British decriminalisation order (article says 2000) but a muted, not 'out and proud' scene rooted in that imposed colonial legacy rather than local choice; notes roughly 15,000 residents as one reason the gay scene stays small.

records.name: Montserrat
records.current_summary:
Same-sex activity is legal in Montserrat: its prohibitions were swept away in January 2001 by the same Order in Council that overrode the region's reluctant legislatures — the earlier claim of 'archaic criminal provisions on the books' was contradicted by the territory's own sources and has been removed. What public LGBT life existed was effectively extinguished twice by disaster: the 1989 hurricane and the 1995 volcanic eruptions that buried the southern half of the island and depopulated it, leaving a scatter of survivors in the north and a gay presence described as 'decimated', only partially recovered.

Local religious leaders called the 2001 reform 'totally unacceptable,' and the territory appeared resigned to following London's order. Visitors today find a tiny, dispersed, private society where neither hostility nor community is much visible.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption that wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north; gay life barely exists locally ('gays are everywhere but hardly here') — decimated social scene; dated but concrete.

Associated Press report (Jan 2001, via GLAPN): Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, saying they violated signed international human rights agreements — the legal basis on which Montserrat's prohibitions were eventually swept away; local politicians and religious leaders opposed, framed as a cultural rift with London.

records.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
records.current_summary:
Turks and Caicos decriminalised same-sex activity in 2001 through the UK-imposed Caribbean reform, and its constitution now bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The live frontier has been recognition rather than criminal law: the Court of Appeal ordered a residence permit for the same-sex spouse lawfully married abroad, holding that 'spouse' in the immigration ordinance must include same-sex spouses and declaring violations of the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees — while declining to touch the constitution's male-female marriage definition, which it treated as controlling.

The administering state's passport guidance maintains a standing profile of the territory's rules on marriage, civil partnerships, adoption and gender recognition. Socially, a resident's account described 'virtually nothing' documented about gay life — in a territory where around two-thirds of inhabitants are themselves not native-born — so visitor experience runs on privacy and the resort economy rather than any visible scene.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz resident account ('Eddi', May 2009): documents how invisible gay life is — 'virtually nothing on the Internet about gay life in TCI'; notes ~2/3 of residents are not originally from the islands and full-citizen Belongers are a demographic minority versus foreigners, so there is no visible scene and privacy is the norm; useful as the on-the-ground social-climate read for a visitor.

UK HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile (Crown copyright 2025): official operational guidance covering nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, and documents for the territory — states adoption is legal and that 'transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands', i.e. the administering state's passport office handles gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction.

TC Weekly News: Court of Appeal landmark ruling ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar — refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened constitutional guarantees; 'spouse' in the Immigration Ordinance read to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, with equality/non-discrimination/private-life guarantees invoked (marriage definition left untouched). Directly relevant: same-sex partners of visitors/residents get residence recognition.

Klshepedia overview (published Apr 2026): same-sex sexual activity legal in the Turks and Caicos Islands since 2001 and discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is constitutionally banned — the two anchor legal facts for a visitor assessing exposure.

records.name: Falkland Islands
records.current_summary:
South Atlantic island settlement with its own assembly: same-sex activity legal since 1989, equal age of consent since 2005, and full equality in April 2017 when the assembly approved same-sex marriage and civil partnerships 7-1, on a public consultation showing 90 per cent support for marriage and 94 per cent for partnerships — the registrar confirmed the law the following June, adoption followed the same year, the constitution bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and the first Pride was held in the capital that April. An official of the community described it as 'open, tolerant and respectful'; note that the much more remote dependencies administered from the same capital did not follow on marriage.

The earlier profile's inherited arithmetic and its borrowed UK custody stories have been deleted: on the surviving evidence the legal picture here is stronger, not weaker, than the administering state's, and there is no source indicating the GB single-sex-services code extends to the territory.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: PinkNews (12 Apr 2017): the Legislative Assembly passed same-sex marriage (7-1) plus civil partnerships open to same-sex AND opposite-sex couples, after a public consultation showing 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in the ~3,000-resident territory — the operative equality reform.

Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): direct confirmation from the Falklands registrar general that the March-passed same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill is law (royal-assent confusion resolved by her reply); same registrar confirms same-sex marriage is NOT legal in the South Georgia and South South Sandwich Islands dependency.

Mirror summary of the Wikipedia LGBTQ rights page (wiki-derived): legal since 1989, equal age of consent since 2005; same-sex marriage and civil partnerships since 29 April 2017; stepchild and joint adoption since 2017; constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination; UK responsible for defence; attitudes largely positive (90% consultation support).

records.name: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
records.current_summary:
A scattered South Atlantic territory of three island groups that legislated equality island by island: the 2009 constitutional order imposed by the administering state bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation across all three, and equal age of consent sits at 16. Marriage equality arrived in staggered fashion — the first dependency's council approved the ordinance 5-0 in May 2016 and it commenced January 2017, the most remote island followed in August 2017, and the principal island itself completed the set on 20 December 2017 — with adoption law following the same year.

The earlier profile undersold all of this as 'decriminalised' and added an unsourced 'church-conservative' gloss; neither survives the evidence. What is documented is a fast, orderly rights rollout across very small councils, and a total absence of survey data on social attitudes — remoteness, not resistance, is the characterised condition.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: Alchetron mirror of the territory's LGBT-rights page (updated 25 Apr 2026): same-sex sexual activity legal; discrimination protections in force since 2009; same-sex marriage legal on Ascension Island since 2017 — the marriage-law jurisdiction of the territory.

GayLawNet laws index for the territory (page accessed 23 Jun 2013, citing ILGA State-sponsored Homophobia): consensual same-sex relations became lawful in 2001 and the age of consent is equalised at 16 territory-wide; page frames the territory as an Overseas Country or Territory of the EU (Charter applicability).

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - discrimination banned territory-wide since 2009; same-sex marriage legal since 2017 (Ascension 1 Jan, Tristan da Cunha 4 Aug, Saint Helena 20 Dec); adoption since 2017; detailed vote records of the Ascension Island Council (5-0).

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror, redirects to the territory article): LGBTQ rights on Ascension Island - the marriage ordinance approved 31 May 2016 (5-0), signed and gazetted 20 June, commenced 1 January 2017.

records.name: Pitcairn Islands
records.current_summary:
Pitcairn's roughly fifty inhabitants govern family law themselves, and on paper they have adopted the most complete equality package in this group of territories: activity legal since 2001, a 2010 constitution that bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and a 2015 Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance — marriage defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, orientation or gender identity, foreign civil partnerships recognised, and adoption open to married, unmarried and single people alike.

The earlier profile's 'Christian-conservative, no public LGBT life' clause appeared in no source and has been deleted; it was the only stated basis for placing this territory below its administering state, which the legal record does not support. What the sources do say is that no islander is known to be in a same-sex relationship — on an island this size, invisibility is arithmetic rather than atmosphere, and defence is the administering state's responsibility.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: Alchetron mirror of the Wikipedia article (updated 25 Apr 2026): Pitcairn Islands (British overseas territory) — same-sex activity legal since 2001; 2010 Constitution bans sexual-orientation discrimination (protections 'since 2010'); same-sex marriage legal since 14 May 2015 and adoption since 2015; none of c. 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship; military service under UK responsibility.

Readable Wiki mirror (Wikipedia, CC BY-SA): discrimination on sexual orientation banned by the 2010 Pitcairn Constitution Order; marriage defined as union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity; same-sex marriage legal since 14 May 2015; the Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 also recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn; adoption open to married, unmarried and single people.

Full Wikipedia republication: same-sex sexual activity legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001; anti-discrimination constitutional protection from the 2010 Constitution Order; same-sex marriage legal 14 May 2015 — ordinance unanimously approved by the Island Council 1 Apr 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair 5 May, published 13 May 2015; adoption legal since 2015; page also indexes the territory within UK LGBT-rights timelines.

records.name: Guernsey
records.current_summary:
A self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, Guernsey moved briskly through the 2010s: in 2011 it aligned blood-donation rules with the metropole, ending the HIV-era ban on gay and bisexual donors; in June 2015 the states rewrote the adoption law to open adoption to same-sex couples, removing a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples; and in December 2015 the states approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting civil-partnership and secular-union alternatives as insufficient, with the law itself commencing from spring 2018.

That record covers sexual orientation squarely; the position on gender identity was asserted in the earlier profile without any cited source and has been deleted, so a transgender visitor should treat legal gender recognition and trans-specific protection as unestablished here — the more notable local quirk being that, on the documented chronology, civil partnership arrived later than in the neighbouring dependency that shares the island group's institutions.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: Guernsey Billet d'État (24 June 2015): official States of Guernsey legislative business document - includes the review of Adoption Law (p.1170) that led to same-sex couples' adoption rights.

BBC (10 Dec 2015): States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting both civil-partnership-only and single 'Union Civile' alternatives; implementing legislation separate and not expected before 2017. Charity Liberate: 'historic day'; debate described as 'extremely positive'.

BBC (24 Jun 2015): Guernsey repealed its 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting — States agreed same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners (Jersey had approved the same change two days earlier).

BBC (23 Sep 2011): Guernsey adopted the UK's relaxed blood-donor rules — gay/bisexual men eligible after 12-month deferral, targeted ~7 Nov 2011 to match the UK change, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions unchanged.

records.name: Isle of Man
records.current_summary:
Isle of Man: a self-legislating Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea whose parliament, Tynwald, works through its own bills on these questions. The House of Keys in 2005 proactively adopted a clause protecting employees from dismissal over sexual orientation, framing it in human-rights terms; the chief minister publicly committed to marriage equality in 2015, at a time when this parliament and Northern Ireland's assembly were the only British legislatures refusing it; the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill passed its final legislative stages in April 2016 and the first civil partnership was converted to marriage that July, preserving the couple's 2015 wedding date.

Current reference material confirms the settled picture: civil partnerships from 2011, marriage since 2016, and a legal gender-recognition right in force since 2009 alongside 'gender reassignment' protections in island equality law. Claims about the metropole's single-sex code and its statutory guidance were carried in the earlier profile without primary legislative support and have been deleted, leaving the local record as the basis of this entry.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of United Kingdom; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: Tynwald Hansard (26 April 2016): Legislative Council proceedings - Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 (same-sex marriage) and consideration of the Equality Bill 2016 - the primary legislative record of the Isle of Man's marriage-equality debate.

BBC (28 Jul 2016): same-sex marriage took effect on the island after Royal Assent of the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act (2015-16 law reform); the first civil-partnership-to-marriage conversion was completed days after entry into force, with civil partnerships (legal since 2011) convertible without a second ceremony — confirming a smooth, routine registration process for couples.

BBC (30 Nov 2005): the House of Keys adopted an Employment Bill amendment protecting gay and lesbian employees from dismissal on sexual-orientation grounds (tabling by Onchan MHK Peter Karran) — the island's employment non-discrimination milestone, aligned with UK human-rights law.

3FM (9 Jun 2015): Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition — the political commitment that preceded the 2016 Marriage and Civil Partnership Act.

freshness_all.fact: Stable: civil partnerships 2011, same-sex marriage since 2016 (the 2015-16 legalisation completed), gender-recognition right since 2009, 'gender reassignment' protections
